- *This is the word of the LORD*: The book of Hosea starts by stating that these are not just human words but a message from the one true God (compare {{Joel 1:1|Joel 1:1}}; {{Micah 1:1|Micah 1:1}}; {{Zephaniah 1:1|Zephaniah 1:1}}). 

- *Hosea son of Beeri*: Several other important people in the Old Testament are also named Hosea (or Hoshea; both names are spelled the same in Hebrew; {{Numbers 13:8|Numbers 13:8}}; {{2 Kings 17:1|2 Kings 17:1}}). Hosea means “the Lord saves,” which is a fitting name for this prophet. 

- *Jeroboam … king of Israel*: Hosea gave prophecies to the northern kingdom of Israel during the reigns of its last seven kings. However, only one of them, Jeroboam II, is mentioned here (see Hosea Book Introduction, “Setting”).
B

Hosea brought messages of judgement and hope to the people of the northern kingdom. He spoke some messages as poems and shared some messages through actions of prophecy.

Hosea obeyed God’s instructions about who to marry and what to name their children. His marriage and the naming of his children were actions of prophecy. Hosea married a woman who had sex with other men. She acted like a prostitute. This was a picture of how the people of the northern kingdom treated God.

God was faithful to them like Hosea was faithful to his wife Gomer. But the people weren’t faithful to God just like Gomer wasn’t faithful to Hosea. Faithfulness between Hosea and Gomer meant having sex only with each other. Faithfulness between God and God’s people meant that God’s people worshipped only God. It meant that they obeyed the Law of Moses recorded in the Mount Sinai covenant.

Hosea gave his children names that meant Not Loved and Not My People. These names were a picture of how God would treat his people. He would treat them as if they weren’t his people that he loved. This means that he would treat them as if the Mount Sinai covenant were broken. The covenant showed that God chose the family line of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He chose them to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. That was how God showed his love for them.

But the people of the northern kingdom worshipped the false god called Baal. It was as if they had forgotten that God was their God. God never stopped being faithful to his people. God promised that one day Israel would recognise him as the Lord. God’s people would enjoy the covenant blessings. They would be led by a king from David’s family line.

Jews came to understand these messages of hope as prophecies about the messiah. New Testament writers came to understand that Jesus is the Messiah.
T

*a prostitute*: Some find it hard to believe that God would tell a prophet to marry a prostitute. Because of this, many interpret this story symbolically. Early church members often thought the marriage did not actually happen. They saw it as an allegory, with Hosea representing the Lord and Gomer representing Israel. 

Today, most believe the marriage was real, but they have different views on Gomer’s job before marriage. Some think Gomer was a regular prostitute, while others believe she was a sacred prostitute in Canaanite fertility worship. Others think Gomer was a young woman who had not yet engaged in illicit sexual activity, but God knew she was likely to commit adultery and prostitution.

- The name Lo-ammi delivers the harshest judgment because it suggests the end of Israel's covenant with the Lord. The title "my people," given to Israel when they obeyed the Lord their God ({{Leviticus 26:12|Leviticus 26:12}}; see also {{Exodus 6:7|Exodus 6:7}}), was now taken away due to their clear unfaithfulness. 

- *I am not your God*: The Hebrew phrase can be translated as *I am not ‘*I Am*’ for you* (compare {{Exodus 3:14|Exodus 3:14}}). The third child's name prophetically states that the Israelites are outside the covenant and can no longer call upon the I Am.

- *the sand of the sea*: This promise of future population growth for God's people repeats the promise given to the patriarchs Abraham and Jacob ({{Genesis 22:17|Genesis 22:17}}; {{Genesis 32:12|32:12}}). 

- *they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’*: This phrase is unique in the Old Testament, but Paul quoted it ({{Romans 9:26|Romans 9:26}}) to show that God had also called the gentiles (non-Jewsish people) to salvation.

These verses show a sudden change in Hosea’s prophecy from judgment to hope. In the next three verses, Hosea changes the names of Gomer’s three children from symbols of divine punishment on Israel to symbols of blessing and hope. This clearly shows God’s power to reverse situations from darkness to light, judgment to hope, and even death to life.

- *Judah and of Israel will be gathered together*: For nearly 200 years, Israel and Judah were separate kingdoms due to political rivalry. When God restores his people, he will reunite these kingdoms under one leader, like in David's time. He will also end the curse of exile (see also {{Ezekiel 37:15-28|Ezekiel 37:15–28}}).

- *the day of Jezreel*: Hosea said that in the future, God would restore Jezreel's original meaning. It will represent blessing and growth instead of judgment.

- *My people*: God will restore the third child's name to its original meaning. 

- *My loved one*: Israel will again receive God's love and compassion.

*Rebuke your mother, rebuke her*: At first glance, the Lord, like an upset husband, seems to be giving a divorce to his unfaithful wife, Israel (see {{Deuteronomy 24:1|Deuteronomy 24:1}}). However, as the passage continues, it becomes clear that God’s goal in this lawsuit is not divorce, but reconciliation ({{Hosea 2:14-23|Hosea 2:14–23}}). 

God’s case against Israel aims to make Israel aware of her sin and offer her a chance to return to her true husband. The Lord’s desire for reconciliation with Israel is surprising because the law required the death penalty for an unfaithful spouse ({{Deuteronomy 22:22|Deuteronomy 22:22}}; see also {{Genesis 38:24|Genesis 38:24}}; {{Leviticus 21:9|Leviticus 21:9}}).

The Lord warns unfaithful Israel that unless she repents and returns to her covenant partner, he will expose her nakedness (see also {{Hosea 2:10|Hosea 2:10}}). Ezekiel also uses this image of judgment and shame ({{Ezekiel 16:36-37|Ezekiel 16:36–37}}).

The only evidence needed to prove Israel’s unfaithfulness comes from her own words: *I will go after my lovers*. Israel’s lovers were the Canaanite fertility deities, especially the *baals* (local representations of the god Baal). The Israelites worshiped them because they believed these gods controlled nature's reproductive forces. The Israelites attributed to them the basic necessities of life: food, water, clothing of wool and linen, and oil used for both sacred and everyday purposes.
